title: Associative memory: total storage, active access and retention
objective: Prove a new, useful theorem giving an associative-memory architecture a quantified advantage in total memory, active read/write cost or retention over the strongest applicable published methods, while preserving high-dimensional queries and cross-coordinate binding.
relationship_to_previous_goal: This explicitly requested goal supersedes the blocked algebraic-complexity objective as the active research task. Historical records, manuscripts and priority uncertainties are preserved without claiming that the old objective was achieved.

Audit primary theorems for sparse inverse/local correction and dynamic graphical inference; classify what is already a known corollary.

Choose a concrete higher-dimensional binding workload for which dynamic dictionaries do not already solve the complete query specification. Seek a better constructive storage/access/retention bound, including changes to the active key set.
Derive a matching obstruction or a substantive separation against the strongest applicable published guarantee, including preprocessing, metadata, precision and encoder costs.
Produce a complete uniform proof and independent exact certificates; audit novelty and all boundary cases before training.
Prepare an honestly scoped manuscript only if novelty and impact gates pass. Use model experiments subsequently to assess the proven practical regime.

acceptance_criteria: A complete uniform proof with explicit hypotheses and a substantive new guarantee beyond the strongest primary baseline.
High-dimensional queries and useful cross-coordinate binding; no silent two-scalar bottleneck or arbitrary-label low-rank assumption.
All stored values, keys, codebooks, index/metadata, parameters, precision and preprocessing are charged.
Overwrite, forgetting, query robustness and horizon assumptions are explicit; no unlimited-precision capacity argument.
Exact reproducible certificates support the proof; numerical agreement alone does not establish it.
A defensible novelty boundary and a useful consequence support an honest paper; known reformulations and baseline separations alone do not complete the goal.

proved_baselines: At least n*log2(alphabet_size) bits are needed to retain n independently replaceable values at known keys.
For fixed linear reads F and write support T, optimal off-target squared interference for a unit target change is (1-ell_i(T))/ell_i(T), with ell a projection leverage score.
If every row deletion of F has all column sets of size at most n-1 independent, an exact isolated overwrite needs at least n changed cells even with redundant state width.
An n-by-n Hadamard read basis has the sharp frontier n/t-1 for t changed cells.

For fixed sparse features with ||I-alpha*F*F^T||_infinity=rho<1, local polynomial correction gives uniform-in-horizon retention error at most rho^(L+1) times the bound on latest values. Metadata and the latest-value cache are charged.

With fixed alpha and uniformly contracting active Gram matrices, a one-row key edit changes only encoding columns in the radius-L ball of the union of old/new overlap graphs. Local column replacement maintains the current polynomial encoding exactly under bounded-capacity insert/delete/replace and value edits.
